extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology (seminarians, theologians)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Catholic doctrinal positions and controversies about sanctifying (habitual) grace: its ontological status, effects (baptism, virtues, adoption), relation to nature, certainty of possession, and growth. The material cites Scripture, Church Councils (Trent), and major theologians (Aquinas, Suarez, Bellarmine, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of baptism in infants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether baptism in infants merely remits guilt or also confers sanctifying grace and infused virtues/habitus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two opposing theological opinions are reported: some say baptism remits guilt but does not confer grace; others assert that guilt is remitted and sanctifying grace and informing virtues are infused (perhaps as habitus even if not presently used). The author regards the second view as more probable and consonant with Fathers and modern theologians, and with the approving conciliar definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological status of sanctifying grace (not a substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace is supra-natural and cannot be a substance or substantial form of the soul; it is to be understood as an accidental form (a quality) of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited texts (Summa Theol., De Veritate) argue: 'quia gratia est supra naturam humanam, non potest esse quod sit substantia aut forma substantialis, sed est forma accidentalis ipsius animae.' The view that treats grace as an absolute accident (sustained independently of the soul) is rejected as extreme and unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratia as a habitual quality/habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratia is classifiable in the first species of quality and, broadly understood, may be treated as a habitual quality (habitus) that perfects the soul though it is not an act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: De Veritate, De Gratia; discussion acknowledges terminological caution about 'habitus' but permits calling sanctifying grace a habitus in a broad sense because it perfects the soul toward a spiritual being and disposes to acts. Suarez noted that denying grace is a habit would not be heretical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation of the divine nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctifying grace is a participation (participatio) in the divine nature, making the soul a sharer in the divine life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by patristic and scholastic sources: 'participationem deitatis' and scriptural references (2 Pet. I, 4). Suarez and others develop that habitual grace elevates created intellectual nature to a participation of a higher divine intellectuality enabling an immediate intuitive knowledge of divine object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infusion of the theological virtues with justification
rubrics_metrics.description: With justification the theological virtues (faith, hope, charity) are infused and adhere in the soul; habitual charity is of faith and its infusion with sanctifying grace is of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciliar and scholastic citations: Council of Trent (Sess. VI, cap. 7), Denzinger-Bannwart; the infusion of faith, hope, and charity occurs simultaneously with justification and their habitual status is affirmed, though some nuance exists about whether they are 'habitus operativi'. Denial of infused charity in justification (excluding grace and charity) is censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between theological virtues and natural principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological virtues presuppose and correspond to natural principles in the soul; God confers divine habits proportionate to these virtues as natural principles correspond to moral/intellectual virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summa Theol. citation: virtues proceed from preexisting natural principles; analogously, God gives habits causing the theological virtues; there should be proportion between these habits and the theological virtues as between natural principles and acquired virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven gifts of the Holy Ghost and the twelve fruits are distinct divine dispositions connected with sanctifying grace and the beatitudes, enabling special operations and perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to St. Thomas and scholastics on the septenarium (seven gifts) and their relation to heroic actions and beatitudes; students are referred to further specialized works for details (e.g., Kleutgen, Schiffini).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoptive sonship and friendship with God
rubrics_metrics.description: By sanctifying grace the justified are made adoptive children and friends of God, distinct from the unique Sonship of Christ; this adoptive sonship is gratuitous and confers participatory dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations (Rom. VIII, John I) and patristic/scholastic exegesis distinguish natural generation from gratuitous adoption. The notion of friendship (amicitia) with God is developed with references to ethical treatments of friendship (Aristotle, Aquinas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctification as interior renewal accompanying remission
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification is not mere remission of sins but includes sanctification and interior renewal of the person through voluntary reception of grace and gifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent (Sess. VI, cap. 7) is cited: 'non est sola peccatorum remissio, sed et sanctificatio et renovatio interioris hominis per voluntariam susceptionem gratiae et donorum.' The point underlines that justification brings multiple simultaneous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase and growth of justification through good works
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification can increase and grow in the justified by cooperation and good works; good works are causes that augment justification rather than being mere signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Trent (Sess. VI, cap. 10), can. 24 (anathema against denying increase), and Aquinas on growth in justice. The Church prays for an increase of faith, hope, and charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of asserting infallible certitude of perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to claim with absolute and infallible certitude that one will certainly have the gift of perseverance until death unless revealed specially; likewise one should not presume to declare oneself certainly justified without any doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent canons cited (can. 16, cap. 9); Denzinger-Bannwart notes anathemas against such presumptions. Pastors and faithful are warned about temerity in asserting absolute certainty of possessing grace or final perseverance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible uncertainty and moral indicators of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: While absolute certitude is precluded, moral certitude of having grace may be inferred from signs (e.g., presence of charity) though interior certainty remains limited; pastoral authors discuss criteria for probable possession of charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aquinas and patristic texts referenced: 'Nemo interroget hominem, redeat unusquisque ad cor suum; si ibi invenerit caritatem fraternam, securus sit.' The text distinguishes between certitude of faith and scruples about personal sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in the measure of grace among the faithful
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is distributed to persons in differing measures according to the gift of Christ and the dispositional capacity of each person; some have more, some less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural support (Eph. IV, 7; Apoc. XXII) and scholastic commentary: 'Unicuique nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi.' The text rejects a uniform measure of grace and explains accidental nature of increase/decrease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of views that deny qualities/faculties in the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical systems (e.g., Herbart) that deny soul qualities and faculties are addressed and criticized for undermining theological accounts of grace and virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to contemporary (for the text) critics and theologians; students are directed to Heinrich-Gutberlet and others for fuller treatment. The passage uses this to defend the scholastic framework that grounds grace as a quality/habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between created and uncreated charity
rubrics_metrics.description: In justification a double charity is given: created charity (whereby we love) and uncreated charity (whereby we are loved); though God is present to all by essence, grace is not given to all equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing St. Bonaventure and conciliar texts: 'In iustificatione duplex caritas nobis datur, scil. creata et increata.' The distinction underpins how charity operates in human response and in the divine gift.
